passages.t: Envoys from Cush in papyrus boats
passages.happening:
‘Woe to the land of whirring wings, along the rivers of Cush’ (verse 1), which sends couriers by sea ‘in papyrus vessels on the waters’ (verse 2).

Isaiah sends the messengers home: go back ‘to a people tall and smooth-skinned, to a people widely feared, to a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers’ (verse 2).

Then he speaks to the whole world: ‘All you people of the world and dwellers of the earth, when a banner is raised on the mountains, you will see it; when a ram’s horn sounds, you will hear it’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Cush, often translated Ethiopia in older Bibles, though it is not modern Ethiopia, lay along the Nile south of Egypt, in what is now northern Sudan. Its kings conquered Egypt in the second half of the eighth century BC, beginning with Piye around 728 BC, and ruled it as Egypt's Twenty-Fifth Dynasty for more than half a century. These pharaohs opposed Assyria's advance and encouraged revolts among the small states of the region. Taharqa appears later in Isaiah as Tirhakah, marching out against Sennacherib.

The envoys were probably seeking to draw Judah into a coalition against Assyria, perhaps around the Ashdod revolt of about 713 to 711 BC or the wider revolt after Sargon II died in 705 BC. Papyrus boats were light reed boats used on the Nile. The land of whirring wings may refer to insects of the Nile, or to the sound of a busy, powerful land.

The description of the Cushites is admiring: tall, smooth-skinned, widely feared, powerful. Isaiah does not condemn them. He redirects them. Judah's leaders were tempted to rely on Egypt and Cush against Assyria, a policy Isaiah fought for years. His message: God does not need their alliance.
passages.later: Isaiah warns again in later chapters against trusting Egypt and Cush (Isaiah 20:5). A psalm sees a different future for the same land: ‘Cush will stretch out her hands to God’ (Psalm 68:31).
passages.asks: Powerful envoys came offering an alliance, and the prophet sent them home. Ask what impressive help you are tempted to accept that would replace trust in God. And ask what it would look like to receive people from far away with respect and still say no to their plan.

passages.t: The LORD waits quietly, and gifts come to Zion
passages.happening:
The LORD has told Isaiah, ‘I will quietly look on from My dwelling place, like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest’ (verse 4).

Before the harvest, when the blossom has gone and the grape is ripening, he will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife and remove the branches (verse 5). They will be left to the birds of prey and wild animals through summer and winter (verse 6).

At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts from that same people, tall and smooth-skinned, widely feared, of strange speech, ‘to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
God's stillness is not absence. He watches, as quiet as heat shimmering in the sun or dew in harvest time, and he acts when the moment is ripe. A vinedresser cuts off shoots before the harvest. So God will cut off the enemy, Assyria, at the right time.

That happened in 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army was turned back from Jerusalem, though the Assyrians defeated an Egyptian and Cushite force at Eltekeh that same year and later invaded Egypt itself.

The chapter ends with one of Isaiah's great visions of the nations coming to Zion. The people who came offering an alliance will come again, bringing gifts to the LORD. The first hearers were shown a future in which a distant, feared nation is drawn not into Judah's wars but into its worship.
passages.later: Zephaniah promises the same: ‘From beyond the rivers of Cush My worshipers, My scattered people, will bring Me an offering’ (Zephaniah 3:10).
passages.asks: God watches quietly and acts when the moment is ripe. Ask whether you can bear God's quiet when you want him to act now. And ask who you think of as too far away or too foreign to come to worship, and what this chapter says about them.
